entries.title: What their hands keep trying
entries.summary: Davies’s hand activities follow familiar movements: fitting, releasing, turning, and using two hands together. The useful choice is the movement your child wants to repeat.
entries.cue: They may be returning to the same lid, shape, peg, or ring.

entries.title: Sing, move, and answer a rhythm

detail: Davies includes spontaneous songs with actions, family and cultural dances, and copying the rhythm a child makes. You can make room for their response as well as offer your own.

entries.title: Read the book they bring back

detail: Davies favors books connected to daily life and a child’s interests, with room for families, cultures, and experiences different from your own. Simple words or sentences can grow into longer stories as interest changes.
Show a slow page turn and careful return to the shelf. Keep a few covers visible in a basket or on a shelf so your child can choose.

entries.title: Leave room for their reply
entries.summary: Your toddler can join a conversation through sounds, gestures, and words. Pause, listen, and respond to what they are trying to share.
entries.cue: They may point, repeat a sound, show you something, or begin a sentence.
detail: In an ordinary moment, name what you are doing or what your child notices. If you do not know the name of a bird or vehicle, you can find out together.
Give them time instead of finishing their sentence. If the meaning is unclear, invite them to show you. You can use the full word naturally in your response without making them repeat it.
Davies suggests coming to the child’s level and showing interest with your body and speech; the appendix qualifies eye contact by cultural appropriateness. Moments of silence belong in the day too.

entries.cue: Notice interest in naming things, recognizing pictures, or finding a familiar object in a book.
detail: Davies groups vocabulary objects around a familiar theme. A photograph of the actual object can make the match clear; a similar but different picture is a later challenge once identical matching is familiar.

Say the names and enjoy finding a match. If an object lands on a different picture, notice it without turning the moment into a test, and return to naming another time. The book reserves its formal naming test for children over 3.

entries.summary: Let your child try a small part of dressing, with help when it is wanted or needed. The amount they want to do can change from day to day.

detail: Davies suggests easy openings and clothes that allow movement, with a limited choice of seasonally suitable things within reach. Elastic waists and a roomy neck opening are examples.

Break dressing into small parts. You might put a shirt over their head and leave the sleeves for them to try, or hold the back of a shoe while they put a foot in. Offer a little help when they are becoming frustrated.
When you must leave, acknowledge the wish to do it alone and explain that you will help finish. Davies keeps gentle handling and connection alongside the adult’s time boundary.

entries.title: The conversation inside everyday care
entries.summary: Davies treats dressing, washing, diapering, and meals as moments to be with a child. She keeps respectful touch and communication within necessary care.
entries.cue: There may be a glance, gesture, sound, or small part of the routine your child wants to join.
detail: She describes talking about what is happening, listening even before words, and allowing the child a turn in the exchange. An ordinary care moment can include a smile and shared attention.
Her respect for a child’s say in touch sits alongside the adult’s responsibility for necessary care and protection. She describes gentle help and brief explanation when care must happen.

entries.title: A familiar order to the day
entries.summary: A recognizable sequence can help your child know what comes next. Davies allows the rhythm to follow the child and the family, without keeping every minute fixed.
entries.cue: Transitions may be harder when the day unfolds differently from what your child expects.
detail: Look at the order your days already tend to follow. A few pictures of the morning or bedtime steps can help you and your child look together at what comes next.
Davies suggests making that picture list with the child. Drawings or photographs can work, and movable pictures can leave room to vary the order.
Her example day is one family rhythm, not a timetable. When a day changes, she suggests anticipating that the difference may be difficult and offering preparation and understanding.

entries.title: Small things your family returns to
entries.summary: A familiar song, weekly outing, or seasonal tradition can become something you share and look forward to. Davies keeps family rituals simple and personal.
entries.cue: Notice which ordinary moments your family already repeats and enjoys.
detail: She includes birthdays and holidays alongside a weekly park visit or a special breakfast. Food, songs, people, and things you make can carry a family’s cultures into daily life.
Her own celebrations draw on more than one tradition and remain inexpensive and low-key. Being together matters more than making the occasion elaborate.

entries.title: Mealtimes as shared time
entries.summary: Davies describes meals as connection as well as nourishment, with the adult arranging what is offered and the child participating at their own pace. She also says food concerns belong with a doctor.
entries.cue: Meals may have become tense, or you may be wondering how much your toddler can join.
detail: In her approach, adults decide what, when, and where food is offered, while the child chooses how much to eat. She favors sitting together when feasible, including a small meal for an adult whose own dinner is later.
She does not expect a toddler to remain until everyone finishes. Her examples keep food and cutlery at the table and allow an adult to help with the parts of eating the child cannot yet manage.

The chapter contains strong assurances about appetite and a separate mealtime-reset method. Its medical qualification is important: Davies asks readers to consider medical or other food-related reasons for refusal and consult a doctor for any concern.

references.locator: Complete adult roles, table participation, cutlery, appetite/reset context and medical note

entries.title: When food goes on the floor
entries.summary: Davies treats food throwing as a moment to understand and set a limit. She suggests asking whether the child is finished, rather than assuming every throw means the same thing.
entries.cue: Food is being dropped or thrown, and you are trying to understand what happens next.
detail: Her example offers an “all finished” gesture and help carrying the plate to the kitchen. If throwing continues, she describes ending that use of the plate calmly, without a threat.

The wider eating section remains relevant: her aim is shared meals and child participation, with medical or other food-related concerns taken seriously. The example is not a way to decide that a child has eaten enough.

entries.title: What bedtime asks of your family
entries.summary: Davies frames sleep as a personal family question, with a familiar bedtime sequence and the help the child needs. She advises specialist help when continuing difficulties affect the child or family.
entries.cue: You may be considering whether the current bedtime or sleeping arrangement is working for everyone.
detail: Her bedtime discussion makes space for ordinary care, books, and conversation before sleep. She explicitly rejects leaving a child to cry alone and notes that illness or teething may call for additional support.
The chapter also describes particular settling methods, sleeping spaces, and changes to feeding at night. Those passages depend on more than a toddler’s age and are not a general bedtime recipe.
Her closing advice is to see a sleep specialist when persistent difficulty affects the well-being of the child or family.

entries.title: Joining in with brushing teeth
entries.summary: Davies approaches teeth brushing through participation and gentle adult help. She is explicit that the book is applying Montessori principles, not presenting official Montessori dental guidelines.
entries.cue: Your child may want to hold the brush, choose part of the routine, or resist help.
detail: Her examples include choosing a toothbrush, deciding when within the bath routine to brush, and brushing alongside an adult. She treats brushing as necessary care while looking for ways the child can take part.
The adult remains involved: the appendix offers a child the first turn and the adult a turn to finish. The chapter emphasizes gentle, respectful assistance.

entries.title: Toileting without a race
entries.summary: Davies describes learning to use the toilet as gradual and led by readiness, without a set age or forcing. She includes a doctor’s check when a medical issue is suspected.
entries.cue: Your child may pull at a wet or soiled diaper, seek privacy while pooping, or tell you they have peed or pooped.
detail: Davies includes these observations among possible signs of readiness, without setting a deadline. Managing clothes is one of the smaller skills the book describes along the way.

Davies prepares familiar places for clean and soiled clothes and uses matter-of-fact language when a child is wet. Her offers of the potty remain qualified by not interrupting absorbed play and not forcing the child to use it.
The source also discusses overnight changes and stool withholding. Those passages are separate from readiness; she says to check with a doctor if a medical issue is suspected.

entries.title: A change your toddler can hear about
entries.summary: When discussing a young toddler’s pacifier, Davies describes telling the child that a change is coming and giving extra support. The discussion is her approach, not a deadline for this age.
entries.cue: A family may be considering a change and wondering how to include the child.
detail: The book describes a gradual move toward less use and asks the adult to notice whether the child is seeking engagement, closeness, or help settling. Those possibilities are invitations to observe, not certain explanations.

Davies also describes planning the later bedtime change with the child. Her sleep chapter retains support rather than crying alone, and specialist help when persistent difficulties affect the child or family.

entries.title: Help a good moment come to an end
entries.summary: Let your child know a transition is coming and make a small plan for finishing. When you can, wait for a pause in what they are doing.
entries.cue: Leaving the park or stopping a puzzle may be difficult even when the next thing is familiar.
detail: Davies suggests checking that the child heard, then making the ending concrete: one last turn, or a place to save unfinished work. The child need not understand clock time to begin recognizing this pattern.
A small choice or useful job can offer a way to join the transition. Some children do not want choices; those suggestions can be left aside.
If it is time to go, an adult can acknowledge the disappointment and follow through with gentle help. Agreement is an invitation to participate, not a promise that leaving will feel easy.

entries.title: A few words, then time to respond
entries.summary: A short, useful cue can be easier to act on than repeated instructions. Give your child time, and show what you mean if the words are not enough.
entries.cue: You have asked more than once, and your child has not yet begun.
detail: Davies suggests a brief piece of information or a familiar word, such as pointing out where something belongs. Go over and show the place if your child seems unsure.
A pause can leave room for processing. She also suggests saying what the child can do, rather than repeatedly describing what to stop.

For a necessary transition, she states what is happening kindly instead of asking a question with no real choice. Gentle humor is another possibility, such as pretending a child’s shoe fits your foot. None of these needs to work every time.

references.locator: Useful information, one word, positive language, humor, no phase, show action and processing time

entries.title: Let them help think of a way
entries.summary: Describe the problem and leave space for your child’s idea. With a young toddler, you may supply most of the possibilities while they learn how it feels to work something out together.
entries.cue: Two people want different things, or the same difficulty keeps returning.
detail: Davies includes toddlers before fluent speech: they can point, act, or offer something as part of a solution. The adult still leads and keeps necessary limits.
Try a plan you can both live with and return to it if it is not working. A picture or brief note can also show that you heard a concern you cannot address just now.
The book’s notes are occasional aids. They do not replace the adult’s attention or the immediate action needed for safety.

references.locator: Adult leadership, preverbal participation, ideas and revisiting a plan
Moderate use of reminders and notebook acknowledgment
Immediate protection

entries.title: When waiting asks too much
entries.summary: A waiting room or café can leave little room for a toddler’s movement and conversation. Davies suggests preparing something to share and adjusting what you expect of the visit.
entries.cue: Your child is restless while the adults need to wait.
detail: Her examples include favorite books, watching the activity outside an airport window, or a small walk together while waiting in a café.
The adult may need to be available for the child instead of reading or making a call. What helps can change during the visit; the aim is to support the child through the wait.

references.locator: Waiting rooms/cafés/travel, movement, shared noticing and preparation

entries.title: A limit you can explain and keep
entries.summary: Davies favors a few clear limits connected to safety and respectful life together. The adult can keep the limit while understanding the child’s disappointment.
entries.cue: You may notice a rule changing from one moment to the next, or realize a limit needs to be clearer.
detail: Her examples focus on protecting people, belongings, and shared spaces. A response stays connected to what happened, such as putting away a ball that continues to be thrown indoors and trying again later.
Consistency leaves room for thought. Davies suggests revisiting house rules at a neutral time as children grow; if an adult changes their mind in the moment, they can acknowledge it.
Her checklist asks whether the limit is clear, kind, reasonable, and suited to the child’s age and ability, and whether the child can help find a solution.

references.locator: Few house rules, kind follow-through, related responses and protection
Early limits, changed mind, consistency, uncertainty and age/ability fit

entries.title: Stay available through a hard feeling
entries.summary: Davies describes staying available during a tantrum, offering comfort without insisting on touch, and keeping everyone safe. Explanation and repair come after calm.
entries.cue: Your child is overwhelmed by a disappointment, frustration, or a limit.
detail: An offered cuddle may help, or your child may push it away. Davies keeps the adult nearby and available when touch is unwelcome, with immediate action to stop harm.

She suggests noticing situations that can be difficult—frustration, events not going as hoped, wanting control, or trouble communicating—and anticipating them when possible. These are possibilities to understand, not a diagnosis or a promise to prevent every tantrum.
In public, she describes moving out of the way when possible. If the family must leave, she retains gentle adult help and acknowledgment of the child’s experience.

references.section: Acknowledge negative feelings / Dealing with tantrums
references.locator: Complete support, declined touch, public/time qualifications, recap triggers and calm-before-repair
Immediate action for danger

entries.title: Help make things right after calm
entries.summary: After everyone is calm, help your child take a small part in addressing what happened. You can model an apology without requiring them to say one.
entries.cue: Someone has been hurt, belongings were damaged, or a mess needs attention after a difficult moment.
detail: Davies pairs acceptance of feelings with helping make things right. A child can join you to check on another person, offer a tissue, or help gather things that were thrown.
Young toddlers need adult help with this. A sincere apology modeled by you can say more than a required “sorry.” The conversation can also make room for what was difficult for your child.

references.locator: Calm first, practical repair, checking on another person and adult modeling rather than forced apology

entries.title: Room for your toddler beside a new baby
entries.summary: Davies makes room for a toddler’s difficult feelings and ordinary time together when a new baby joins the family. The adult still steps in immediately to prevent harm.
entries.cue: Your toddler may want closeness, want to help, or want little to do with the baby.
detail: The book suggests keeping the early weeks simple and accepting extra hands when available. Books or familiar toys close by can give you something to share with your toddler while feeding the baby.
Fetching a clean diaper may interest a toddler; declining to help is allowed too. A brief walk or ordinary errand together can offer time with you.
If the toddler expresses anger or jealousy, Davies listens rather than denying the feeling. She is equally clear that hitting the baby must be stopped immediately.

references.locator: Post-arrival adjustment, optional helping, books during feeding, feelings, immediate protection and individual time

entries.title: Help both children with the same problem
entries.summary: When siblings disagree, Davies supports both children without choosing a side. Staying neutral still includes stopping harm and giving as much help as the situation needs.
entries.cue: Two children want the same object, or their play is becoming uncomfortable for one of them.
detail: Describe what each child seems to want and the problem between them. A young toddler may communicate with actions, and the adult may offer most of the possible solutions.
Small disagreements may need your visible presence; a situation becoming unsafe needs action. Davies describes separating children to prevent harm, then helping them work on a solution after calm.

Her wider sibling discussion favors responding to each child’s needs rather than making every amount of time identical. Shared enjoyable moments can be welcome without requiring siblings to be close friends.

references.locator: Neutral support, proportional intervention, immediate safety, problem solving, positive interactions and individual needs
Preverbal participation and adult leadership

entries.title: A turn for the child using it, and help waiting
entries.summary: Davies’s home approach gives a child time with an activity and supports the child who wants the next turn. Public places may call for a shorter ending so others can have a turn.
entries.cue: One child is using something another child wants.
detail: At home, she allows repetition rather than requiring a child to hand over the activity immediately. Watch whether another child’s company is welcome, offer simple words for each child’s wish, and step in to stop pushing or grabbing.
The waiting child needs support too. At a shared playground, Davies instead acknowledges the person waiting and gives the current turn a clear ending as a courtesy.
Before visitors arrive, she suggests letting a child put away especially important toys and agreeing that guests may use what remains.

references.locator: Parallel-play framing, home turns, protective help, public-space exception and visitors

entries.title: Time to watch before joining
entries.summary: Let your child stay near you and look around when a social setting feels unfamiliar. Davies offers support without trying to change a quieter temperament.
entries.cue: They may watch from beside you instead of going straight into the group.
detail: Beforehand, describe a little of what will happen. On arrival, show them around or allow time at your side while you carry on an ordinary conversation.

Davies suggests small supported practice when it is useful, such as trying a greeting or words for “stop.” The purpose is helping the child handle a situation, not comparing them with a more outgoing child.
An early arrival or shorter visit is another possibility when a busy group is difficult.

references.locator: Acceptance, preparation, watching, supported social practice and avoiding labels
Tour, early arrival and shorter visits

entries.title: A hug can be offered
entries.summary: Offer affection and notice whether it is welcome. Davies gives children a say in ordinary touch while keeping the adult’s responsibility to protect them.
entries.cue: A child pulls away from a hug, or your enthusiastic toddler approaches another child.
detail: When a child withdraws, you can help the other child notice: they may not want a hug just now. Davies suggests checking rather than demanding affection.

She applies the same respect to adults offering hugs or elective help. Necessary care and immediate protection still call for gentle adult action; a child’s refusal does not remove that responsibility.

references.section: Skills for introverted toddlers / Respectful contact
references.locator: Peer withdrawal, offered hugs and the child’s say in touch
Necessary gentle care and immediate protective action

entries.title: Stop the hurt, then understand the moment
entries.summary: Davies keeps an adult close enough to stop hitting, biting, or pushing. Understanding the feeling goes alongside protecting everyone; repair waits until calm.
entries.cue: There has been physical conflict, or you have noticed situations where it is becoming likely.
detail: Her first response is to stop the harmful action and move children apart when needed. Acknowledging a feeling does not mean allowing the action to continue.

At a calmer time, notice patterns: what was happening, who was nearby, how noisy or crowded it was, and how the adults responded. Davies offers these as clues for adjusting support, not proof of a child’s motive.
After calm, she helps the child check on the other person and models making amends. Laughter does not change the protective limit or prove why the child acted.

references.locator: Protection, observation categories, adjustments, response, repair and laughter
Available comfort, safety and calm before repair

entries.title: An interest in throwing needs a place
entries.summary: Davies responds to throwing by noticing patterns, protecting people and belongings, and finding an appropriate outlet for the movement.
entries.cue: Objects are being pushed from a table or thrown around the room.
detail: She describes moving vulnerable things out of reach and temporarily removing objects that could hurt when thrown—including wooden toys.
Her examples distinguish throwing outside from using soft things indoors. The underlying question is which movement the child is seeking and where it can happen within a clear limit.

references.locator: Patterns, preventing harm, wooden objects and different throwing possibilities
Putting away an indoor-thrown ball and trying later

entries.title: When they want you close
entries.summary: Davies makes room for toddlers who want company. Shared play or a small part of daily work can offer connection while you notice what help they need.
entries.cue: Your child wants to stay beside you, follows you, or asks you to do something together.
detail: Changes, temperament, divided attention, or difficulty managing an activity are among the possibilities Davies considers. None explains every child or every day.
She begins with playing together and gradually watching more while the child leads. She also includes the child in ordinary work, such as handling socks while the adult does laundry.
Toddlers still need supervision and are not expected to play alone for hours. In new places, she suggests helping them get oriented and saying where you are going instead of sneaking away.

references.locator: Possible context, normal supervision, shared play/work, understanding and announced departures

entries.title: A small signal when you are talking
entries.summary: For an ordinary conversation, Davies describes a hand on the adult’s shoulder as a way to say, “I have something to tell you.” The adult acknowledges the child and returns to them at a pause.
entries.cue: Your toddler wants to speak while you are in a conversation.
detail: Her example uses the adult’s hand over the child’s hand to show the message has been received. The adult then pauses as soon as it is appropriate to listen.
It takes practice and does not set a length of time a toddler should wait. This is an ordinary conversation signal, not a condition for getting urgent help.

references.section: Learning how to interrupt an adult
references.locator: Shoulder-hand signal, adult acknowledgment and response at appropriate pause

entries.title: Tell them what you noticed
entries.summary: Specific words can share your interest: a line on the page, a careful movement, or the help your child offered. Davies also makes room for your own delight.
entries.cue: Your child looks to you after doing something, or you want to acknowledge their effort.
detail: The book suggests describing the action instead of giving it a general grade. A warm “I’m excited for you” is among Davies’s examples; this is not a rule to hide affection.
She distinguishes an action from a fixed identity. Describing what happened today leaves more room than calling a child “the clever one,” “the clumsy one,” or “the shy one.”
During absorbed activity, you can wait until the child seeks a response rather than interrupting every step.

references.section: Give our child feedback / Roles and labels
references.locator: Specific action descriptions, expressed warmth, action-level words and fixed labels

entries.title: The experiences Davies wants to leave room for
entries.summary: Davies favors firsthand play, conversation, and shared activity over screens for toddlers. She presents this as part of her Montessori approach and describes her own family’s choices.
entries.cue: You may be considering what fills waiting time or sits in the background at home.
detail: Her practical examples include books or a shared activity when out, a walk to see what is happening nearby, and noticing adults’ own screen use.
Her account also includes occasional selected programs when her children were young. It is not a minute-by-minute plan, and her family’s later computer skills are an anecdote, not a promised result.
For upset feelings, she returns to the support and connection described in her limits chapter.

references.locator: Preference, alternatives, adult modeling and complete personal-experience continuation
Support and connection during distress

entries.title: The languages in your family’s day
entries.summary: Davies describes different ways a multilingual family can make its languages part of everyday life: through particular people, or through familiar places and times.
entries.cue: Your household or caregivers may use more than one language.
detail: One example has adults speaking their own mother tongues with the child and an agreed language together. Another uses different languages in different settings. These are alternatives families can consider, not a demand to use both.
The useful focus is the language children share with real people in daily life. The book’s family anecdote illustrates an arrangement; it does not establish a fluency timetable.

references.locator: One Person One Language, Domains of Use, multilingual family example and surrounding asserted outcomes

entries.title: Make activities easy to see and choose
entries.summary: Set out a few complete activities your child is interested in, with their pieces together and a familiar place to return them.
entries.cue: Notice what gets used, what is too difficult, and what has stopped inviting another turn.
detail: A basket or tray can show what belongs together. Davies sets out a puzzle undone and keeps needed pieces available; an incomplete activity can be put aside until its missing piece is found.
Store unused or currently difficult activities for another time, and rotate when your child is looking for a new challenge. The book does not ask for a fixed number or a rotation schedule.
Show where things belong and share putting them back. If your child is already absorbed in the next activity, Davies sometimes models the return herself.

entries.title: A shared room can serve different ages
entries.summary: Davies describes shared rooms with places for each child’s belongings and privacy. Older children’s small parts stay truly inaccessible to younger children.
entries.cue: One child reaches for another’s work, or a shared room needs clearer places.
detail: Her storage examples keep older children’s small parts genuinely out of younger children’s reach, or in containers the younger child cannot open. If an activity can be simplified for the younger child, that is a separate way to join.
She also describes places for personal belongings and for being alone, with clear agreements about using a shared space. This is different from sending an upset toddler away.
For small homes, fewer displayed items and useful storage can create room. The purpose is a home that works for its people.

entries.title: A place for art to begin and rest
entries.summary: Keep a simple drawing invitation ready, and give wet work or saved work somewhere to go. The space can support making without keeping every piece forever.
entries.cue: Materials are hard to find, or finished drawings keep gathering on the table.
detail: Davies describes toddler art trays with what is needed already together. Independent collecting of a whole set of materials is a later example, around 3 years.

Her options for finished work include a tray for things to return to, a selection in a scrapbook, a photograph of bulky work, or a changing display. Reusing a drawing as wrapping paper is another possibility.
Choose the arrangement that helps your family make and put things away; a separate art room is not part of the invitation.

entries.title: Play with the things already here
entries.summary: Davies makes room at home for open-ended play as well as practical activities. Familiar favorites can be a good place to begin.
entries.cue: Your child may be exploring a toy in a new way or acting out something from ordinary life.
detail: She describes pretend play as one way children process what they experience: cooking, caring for a baby, or taking a trip. It need not become a lesson or a performance for an adult.

Her home examples include blocks, farm animals, trains, and vehicles. These are possibilities within a varied collection, not a shopping list. Materials still need to fit the child using them, with supervision for small parts.
If a child attends a Montessori classroom, she makes room at home for daily life, outdoors, creativity, and rest without duplicating all the school materials.

entries.title: A part in washing hands
entries.summary: Davies includes handwashing among the care routines toddlers can join, with help as their skills grow. The child does not have to manage every part.
entries.cue: Your child may want a turn with the soap, the towel, or a movement they have watched you make.
